title: Tandem apply takes the batch quoted as its argument
paragraphs: `tandem apply '{"blade": {"at": 12.5}}'` used to look for a file called {"blade"..., so agents got "Couldn't read" (the ESLint agent did twice), and the fix `tandem media` suggests for a file's role, written that way, didn't run. An argument starting with { or [ is now the batch itself; a file or - for standard input work as before.

title: A new build is swapped in whole, so tandem never runs half an app
paragraphs: build-app.sh used to delete ~/Applications/Tandem.app and rebuild it in place: copying, making the icon and signing took seconds, and a `tandem` command run then (an agent's, mid-install) found no binary or a half-signed one. Worse, the launcher took a missing binary to mean Tandem wasn't installed and started a second build. The bundle is now built beside the old one and swapped in with two renames (a swap cut short puts the old one back), and the launcher waits up to 5 s for the app before building it.

title: Stickers sit at the bottom of the frame, not over Mike's face
paragraphs: placeMedia used to fit a sticker to the whole frame like a shot, so the ESLint video's "Comment below" (712x484) and "Like and subscribe" (1280x392) landed huge over Mike's face. Stickers now sit at the bottom centre, at most 40% of the frame's width and 30% of its height (the sizes Mike approved there), never above twice their own pixels, 5% of the height in from the edge. `anchor` (bottom, bottomLeft, bottomRight, top, topLeft, topRight, centre, lowerThird) puts one elsewhere or anchors any other picture, and `pop` adds scale keyframes that pop it in and out. `tandem assets use` takes --anchor and --pop, and so does the assets_use MCP tool.

title: Clips can hold their first and last frames past their files
paragraphs: A clip with holdEdges runs past the ends of its media: the first frame holds before the file starts and the last after it ends, with no sound there. It's for B-roll that's a little short for its line, or a shot held under a section card, instead of a PNG still of the last frame (which goes stale when the shot is regenerated). The renderer already held edge frames for transitions; this lets a clip ask for it. Trims can pull a held clip past its file, the timeline hatches the held stretches, the Inspector has a Hold ends switch (turning it off trims the clip back first), `tandem timeline` says how long it holds, and the too-long error says how to use it. Saved only where it's on.

title: Agents keep working through a restart
paragraphs: When Tandem quits (a new build going in), calls already running finish and answer before the API stops, so an edit sent just before still gets its reply. Commands sent while the app is closing or opening the project again wait up to 90 seconds for it instead of 15, and say so on stderr. `tandem watch` and the event stream carry on through the restart, and the app waits up to 30 seconds for a CLI command that has the project when it opens again.

title: Snapshot test comments: run from the repo root
paragraphs: Two doc comments from the monorepo still passed --package-path tools/tandem.

title: Hover works, from AppKit, and buttons answer the pointer
paragraphs: SwiftUI's hover never fires in the editor window, so nothing lit up under the pointer: no button backgrounds, no tile outlines, no scrubbing a sound or a transition preview by hovering it. pointerHover and pointerMoves put a see-through AppKit view over the SwiftUI one that follows the pointer with a tracking area (the timeline's own views work that way) and never takes a click. Every onHover and onContinuousHover now goes through them.

Buttons answer the pointer: the timeline tools, the viewer's transport, small icon buttons, outline buttons and the library tabs get a background, text toggles, sub-tabs and inspector tabs brighten, and Export goes a shade lighter.

title: A transition's sound comes through extracts, templates and quick picks, and clips keep their edges under its box
paragraphs: A review turned up ways a transition's sound could double or come back. An extract, lift or insert through the swoosh cut it, and the sound was put back whole beside the piece the cut left, so its tail played twice; now the pieces a cut makes of a sound go with it (the edit context records where each cut piece came from). A command that names the sound itself, like a ripple delete of it, is left as it did it, even when it moves the cut. Only the clips a command names count, not the clips linked to them, so a roll inside a saved segment still carries its sound. Templates and saved segments keep a transition's sound tied, agents can tie or untie a clip with soundClipID, a clip in a crossfade of its own can't be tied, and the timeline dump says which transition a sound belongs to.

On the timeline, clip edges now win over a transition's edges, so a fade as long as its clip leaves the next cut to trim and roll, and a clip a box all but covers can still be picked above and below the label. The blade cuts through a box. Edges only drag on a box at least four grabs wide, grips don't show on a locked track, and the longest a drag allows keeps both sides on whole frames. Picks in the Sound and Type menus land in the order they were made, a drag's early copy of the sound and its drop share one library use, a drop on a transition asks the picks in Settings like everything else, and tying or untying a sound repaints its clip. A new SFX track takes a number no track has.

title: The review diff's correspondence keeps only what it uses
paragraphs: The projects it was built from were stored but never read after it paired the clips.

title: A headless redo puts an agent's edit back into review
paragraphs: With the app closed, tandem redo restores a whole project from the undo history, which the coordinator only sees as a reload, so a redone agent edit stayed out of the review log while a redo in the app brought it back. The service now tells the recorder what it redid. status's help and its MCP tool description mention the edits waiting for review, and the review snapshot also shows the timeline after Mark reviewed.

title: A transition's menu picks its sound, and a ripple that swallows a sound brings it back
paragraphs: The transition's right-click menu has a Sound submenu (none, or its type's own), as the inspector does. Tests pin two more ways a sound follows its transition: a ripple that takes all of the sound while the clips still meet puts it back whole before the new cut, and a sound on a locked track can't be changed or removed through its transition.

title: Tips are macOS tooltips again, on an AppKit view over each control
paragraphs: SwiftUI's hover never reached the controls in the editor, so neither .help nor Tandem's own hover tips showed, and the full-window layer that drew them may itself have been in the way. An AppKit view's toolTip does show there (the timeline's + Track corner), so each control with a tip gets a see-through AppKit view over it carrying the tooltip: clicks pass through it to the control, and macOS shows the tooltip as usual.

title: A dropped push's swoosh checked end to end, and in an export
paragraphs: A drop now has a test the whole way through the app with a scratch asset library: the light swoosh is copied into the project's assets/sfx by the library (so its use is recorded for credits), goes in with the push as one edit, peaks on the cut at 15 LU under the voice, and the new push is picked. A sound clip's tip on SFX says which transition it belongs to.

A real export of a small generated project (speech either side of a pause, a push at 6 s playing the swoosh) puts the swoosh's loudest moment at 5.999 s and its loudest 400 ms 15.4 LU under the speech, with the file at -14.0 LUFS and true peaks at -2.3 dBTP. docs/ASSETS.md has the numbers and where the project and the script that measured it are.

title: Transitions draw as long as they play, their edges drag their length, and they bring their sounds
paragraphs: Mike asked for Filmora's transition: a box over the ends of both clips that gets wider and narrower as its length changes. A transition now draws as a see-through box over the time it plays, as wide as its length at the zoom and centred on the cut, with its icon and name (and a mark when it plays a sound) in a label under the clips' name badges; picked, it's outlined in amber with grips on its edges. Dragging an edge changes the length with both sides moving together a frame at a time, up to half of each clip, snapping like a trim, with the length beside the pointer and one undo step on release. The cut inside the box still trims and rolls above and below the label, and effects and looks still drop onto the clips under it. A drag or a new length repaints only the boxes and sounds it changed.

Transitions come with the sound their type plays: the light swoosh on push, slide, cut slide and wipe, none on the rest, and Mike picks each type's own in Tandem > Settings. Dropping one, double-clicking it in Effects and Cmd-D copy the sound into the project from the asset library first, so it goes in with the transition as one edit; a new type brings its sound when the old one played its type's or none. The inspector's transition section has a Sound menu (none, its type's, or a favourite or recent sound effect), a level, and a button that picks the sound's clip on SFX, which shows as tied while its transition is picked.

title: The review band and chip use Tandem's own tips
paragraphs: macOS's tooltips never showed in the editor, which is why the app now draws its own. The review chip's buttons use .tip like the rest of the toolbar, and resting on the ruler's band shows who changed what there through the same tip, swapping the words when the pointer moves on to another stretch and putting them away when it leaves the band.

title: Agent edits waiting for review show on the timeline
paragraphs: The review log now shows in a soft violet, clear of the amber that selection and markers use: a band on the ruler over the changed stretches, stronger where changes pile up, with a wedge at each place to stop, and hovering it says who changed what and when ("Claude · Add push · 14:32"). Each changed clip gets a tint and an outline just inside its edge, so a selected clip's amber still shows, and a notch marks each join where something was taken out. A chip in the timeline toolbar shows while anything waits ("5 agent edits"), with previous and next buttons and Mark reviewed, which clears the log. They're commands in the Timeline menu too, on [ and ] and Option-].

The marks over the lanes are views of their own, placed again only when the changes, the clips or the zoom move and scrolled with the lanes, so the lanes' tiles never repaint for them; the ruler redraws when the review changes. Stepping lands on the start of each change, and starts close together share a stop, so a ducked music bed that covers the whole band doesn't swallow the shots over it. Saving a version carries the waiting edits over, and the docs say how agents see what's waiting.

title: A review log of what agents change, kept wherever they edit
paragraphs: Mike asked to see what an agent changed since he last looked, rather than watching the whole video again. Every project session (the app, tandem serve and each headless command) now keeps a review log beside the journal, .tandem/<name>.review.json: each committed batch whose author isn't Mike or Tandem is compared with the project before it and recorded by clip ID, so the record follows its clips through later moves and ripples. It lists the clips added, the clips changed, transitions, and removals, which are marks at the join pinned to the clip after it.

Telling an edit from its side effects is the hard part. The take is the reference: its surviving media maps old times to new ones, so a clip that moved exactly as the take around it rode along with a ripple, the right half of a clip cut in two is the same clip, and a ripple delete is one mark at its join rather than everything after it. A clip put back unchanged with a new ID, which is what an agent rebuilding a track does, is the same clip too: on copies of the ESLint video's export snapshots, a pass that rebuilt 88 B-roll clips comes out as the 16 that changed.

Later edits by anyone carry the highlights along, an undo (in the app or headless) drops what it put back, and agent batches a crash left in the journal are caught up when the project opens. Change events now carry the project before and after, since observers can't read the coordinator from inside a notification. tandem status lists what's waiting as reviewPending, read-only, and archives leave the log out.

title: A transition can carry a sound that goes where it goes
paragraphs: Mike wants a light swoosh on every push. It plays as an ordinary clip on the first free SFX track, so he can see it, nudge it, trim it and turn it down, and the transition holds its ID (soundClipID). After every command the editor keeps the two in step: a transition that goes takes its sound with it (a delete, a clip it joins deleted or rippled away, its clips moved apart, a section card making room at its cut), and one whose middle moves carries its sound whole by the same amount, so rolling the cut or rippling the take never leaves the swoosh behind or chops it. The sound keeps its distance from the transition's middle, where a push moves fastest, so a longer push keeps its swoosh on the cut. Deleting the sound itself leaves the transition silent, and undo brings both back together.

Agents give a sound with addTransition's sound (mediaID, gainDB, offset) or change it with a sound patch in updateTransition (null removes it); the schema, the guide and tandem timeline show it. TransitionSoundDefaults says what each type plays: the light swoosh on push, slide, cut slide and wipe, at -23.3 dB so its loudest 400 ms sits 15 LU under speech, starting 0.39 s early so its loudest moment lands on the cut. One rule for when a transition plays (Transition.window) now serves the render too.

title: Tips find their window, and follow SwiftUI's hover
paragraphs: Mike still saw no tip on the timeline's tools. Each window's tip layer took its window's number when it was built, before the window was on screen and had one, so no tip ever matched a window. The layer now keeps its window's identity, the hover gives the pointer's place in the window directly, and the tip goes in the key window (or the frontmost).

title: Cmd-Shift-A selects everything after the playhead
paragraphs: Filmora's key for it, which Mike reached for. A already did it (as in Premiere); Deselect all keeps Escape. The command reads "Select everything after the playhead" in the Edit menu, and dragging the selection moves it all.

title: Tips that show, SFX waveforms, and the inspector turns to fit a clicked clip
paragraphs: Mike couldn't see tooltips on the timeline's tools. Their words were on every control (VoiceOver read them) but macOS never showed them, so Tandem draws its own: rest on a control for half a second and its words, key included, show beside the pointer, until it leaves, clicks, types or scrolls. Every .help is now .tip.

Sound effects show their waveform like music and the voice, with the name at the top when the lane is tall enough. Clicking a sound clip turns the inspector from Video or Colour to Audio, and a picture with no sound turns it from Audio back to Video.

title: Skip tests the CI runner can't run fairly, keeping them on a Mac
paragraphs: The runner's 1024 x 768 screen can't hold the 1100 x 700 window the placement test opens, so that test now skips when the screen is too small. Three frame-timing and slow-Vision tests failed only from runner jitter. They skip when CI=true unless TANDEM_TIMING_TESTS=1, and still run by default on a Mac.

title: A transition goes on any cut, holding edge frames where a file runs out
paragraphs: Mike couldn't drop a push between a screen recording and a cartoon: the cartoon was used from its first frame, so there was nothing before the cut for the transition's first half, and the drop was refused without a word. As in Premiere and Filmora, a clip with no frames past the cut now holds its edge frame there: the render already held the last frame, and now holds the first (the direct decode path clamps to it too). The edit says which clip holds and for how long. A transition longer than a clip is still refused.

title: Split the font checksum in the API tests' copy of FontFixtures too
paragraphs: TandemAPITests has its own FontFixtures.swift with the same checksum expression, which CI's Xcode 26.6 compiler also timed out on.

title: Split the expressions CI's older Swift can't type-check in time
paragraphs: CI builds with Xcode 26.6, whose type checker is slower than the local Swift 6.4. Three test expressions timed out there. I split those, plus the three next slowest found with -warn-long-expression-type-checking (each 380 to 460ms locally, against 85ms for anything else), into typed intermediate lets. The maths and its order are unchanged.

title: Split matte smoothing arithmetic so CI's compiler can type-check it
paragraphs: The macos-latest runner timed out type-checking the one-line blend in MatteSmoothing.swift. The same maths now uses typed intermediate lets, and so do the two lookup tables in that file with the same nested clamp pattern. Results are unchanged.

title: FitSectionCards refits section cards to their words
paragraphs: Fit to text was only in the app, so an agent updating a video's cards after the lengths grew had no way to do it in one step. fitSectionCards fits every card (or clipIDs): each keeps its start, its end moves without rippling and its whoosh out moves with its sweep out. Cards that fit already are left alone, so a batch with it still works; no cards at all is an error.

title: Section cards are a little longer, and just a number by default
paragraphs: Mike found "SECTION 3 OF 5" beside the chip harder to take in than the number alone, and the cards a bit quick. The kicker was already off by default, but the docs and the command's example passed Section, so agents added it; they now leave it off unless Mike asks. Cards get 0.8 s to take them in on top of the wipes and read at 15 characters a second rather than 17, from 4 s to 7 s: his "The one I would turn on" card goes from 4.1 s (without the kicker) to 5.3 s.

title: A project's timeline reopens where it was
paragraphs: Installing a build restarts Tandem, which put the playhead back at the start and fitted the timeline every time. Each project now keeps its playhead, zoom, scroll and track scroll when its window closes (quitting closes them first) and carries on there when it opens.

title: The timeline's scroll bar stands for the video
paragraphs: With the whole video on screen the thumb filled only two thirds of the bar, since the timeline scrolls on until the end sits mid-screen, which read as more to see. The bar is now the video start to end: the thumb fills it when all of it shows, and shrinks against the end when the lanes run past it.

title: A scroll bar under the timeline
paragraphs: Mike could pan with the middle button but nothing showed where he was. The bar's thumb covers what's on screen out of the whole video, with an amber tick at the playhead. Drag the thumb to scroll, drag either end to zoom (keeping the other end's time put, like Premiere's zoom scroll bar), click the bar to jump there and double-click it to fit the video.

title: Softer section card whooshes, a blinking cursor, and cards as long as their words
paragraphs: Mike liked the wipe but found the whoosh in "a bit jarring", an explosion. Measured, it was: 73% of its energy under 150 Hz, centred at 210 Hz, and rising and falling about 10 dB every 10 ms near its peak. The whoosh out had no boom but a hard, clipped peak. Both are replaced by two takes of one new ElevenLabs prompt for a soft, airy swish, the gentlest two of three by measurement: almost no low end, centred at 1.9 and 2.8 kHz, swelling about 4 to 5 dB every 10 ms. They start with their sweeps, and their gains put their loudest moment 15 LU under speech at -20 LUFS, where Mike's own section swipes sit. AudioLevels.speechLevel says where a project's speech actually plays, and the card's sounds move with it, so an import whose speech plays at -28.7 gets them 8.7 dB quieter. In the first demo that level difference had the whoosh in as loud as the voice.

The title gets a text cursor after its last letter: a bar in the accent, 0.1em wide and the capitals' height, 0.07em after the letter. It comes in with the words, is lit as the title lands, blinks 0.53 s on and off with hard steps and is gone once the wipe out starts. It's the cursor prop, on by default, with a switch in the Video tab, and it's pinned at 1080p and 4K through the compositor, a frame grab and an export.

A card is now as long as its words need: 1.4 s for the wipes, then the title, subtitle and kicker at 17 characters a second (Netflix's pace for adult subtitles), from 3.2 s, so the usual short card stays as it was, to 6 s. addSectionCards, tandem cards and the Templates tile use it unless given a length, each card's whoosh out follows its own sweep, and the Video tab's Fit to text sets it for a card whose words changed, moving the whoosh out with it.

title: No Media heading under the Media tab
paragraphs: With the tabs on the library panel the heading repeated the tab right above it. The + that looks for new files sits beside the search field.

title: The library's tabs sit on the library panel
paragraphs: They only ever changed the left panel, so they're now across its top, with their names when it's wide enough and icons alone when it's narrow. Transitions share the Effects panel (with Looks), so they're its sub-tab rather than a tab of their own, and the Effects tab comes back to whichever of the two was showing. The top bar keeps the name, Agents and Export, and is 8 pt shorter.

title: Section card docs, and insert mode that clears a transition on the section cut
paragraphs: RENDER.md has the section card's design: the layout in cqw, the motion and easing, how the wipes reveal the shots either side, what differs from the mockup on purpose and how the frames were checked against Chrome. ARCHITECTURE.md says where graphic clips and the card's fonts fit, ASSETS.md covers the bundled fonts' licences and the two ElevenLabs whooshes with their prompts, and PLAN.md has the done lines.

addSectionCards in insert mode takes out a transition on the cut at the marker before making room there, and warns about it. The room pulled the transition's clips apart, so on a real edit the whole batch failed with "joins clips that don't meet". The card hides that cut anyway.
SectionCardSnapshots draws a card's Video tab in an offscreen window, and the tile's art, and writes them out as PNGs when TANDEM_CARD_UI_OUT is set.

title: A quieter UI, with icons where words were
paragraphs: Mike asked for less: the title bar is just the video's name (the status bar already says when a save fails), and track names get a picture or sound icon instead of the "cutout · look" and "-20 LUFS" lines under them. Library sub-tabs have icons.

The same pass takes out words the controls already say: the licence under every asset (only an unknown one stays, in red), sources that can't be used yet, "from <folder>/", "camera + screen", "Transcribed" (a tick now), the library and Activity explanations, "Transitions you use most", "Muted No" and "Keep mic On" beside their switches, the clip header's timecode line, the Measured and Plays at rows (now in the Normalise tooltip), an all-levelled speech status and its greyed button, empty effects notes, the idle "not connected" and the status bar's format summary. "Linked camera + screen" is just Linked.

title: Section cards, drawn by Tandem, and a card at every section marker
paragraphs: A section card is now one clip: a graphic clip with the built-in template sectionCard, drawn by the compositor at the output size, so the viewer, paused stills, frame grabs and exports show the same frame, sharp at 4K. It's card B of the title card mockup, Convex's yellow, red and purple bands sweeping across to wipe it in and out, with card D's progress row: a number chip, the title in Anton, a letter-spaced subtitle, a bar for each section (up to six, then one bar in proportion and a count like 3 / 14) and an optional kicker beside the chip (SECTION 1 OF 3). Sizes, fonts, colours, timing and easing are the mockup's; the wipes keep their length and a longer or shorter card holds longer or shorter.

Three things differ from the mockup on purpose. In Chrome its first sweep never showed (the second animation's backwards fill held the bands off screen) and the card popped in; both sweeps play here. The bands travel 372% of their width, since 360% left a purple sliver bottom right. And the card is revealed behind the first band and hidden behind the last, so the wipes show the shots either side instead of switching under the bands. Rendered side by side with the mockup's CSS in headless Chrome, frames match to within a pixel.

Anton, Instrument Sans and JetBrains Mono ship in TandemRender's resources with their OFL licences and load straight into font descriptors, so every process draws the card the same. Other graphic templates still warn.

addSectionCards puts a card at every section marker after 0:00 (or the ones named), numbered in order with the total, titles from the marker names and subtitles from their notes, starting just early enough to hide the frame from the marker on. Cards already at a marker are renumbered and keep their words; insert mode makes room so the card is a pause. Sounds for each sweep go on SFX, linked to their card. tandem cards, the cards MCP tool and POST /v1/cards plan it and apply it with the two whooshes made for the card in the asset library, and so does Timeline > Add section cards at section markers (Option-M) in the app.

The Section card tile in the Text tab shows the rendered card and adds it with its whooshes; the inspector's Video tab edits its title, subtitle, number, total, kicker and colours; the timeline names it by its number and title. Template clips can bring their own media now, and template fields fill graphic text props as well as titles.

title: Live Photo movies travel with their stills, and shared fonts reach every render
paragraphs: Since the merge of tandem, a Live Photo is one media item with its movie in livePhotoVideo. Archiving now counts that movie as one of the project's files: it's copied in beside its still, whether consolidating or archiving with --to, and the item is pointed at the copy, so a scan of the archive still knows it's the still's movie rather than a video of its own. A copy the folder watcher added meanwhile is removed again, as for other copies. Relink takes the movie beside the still it finds, a saved segment copies it, and inserting a segment carries it while its folder still has it.

The text styles work registers a project's assets/font/ in whatever process renders it. The shared library's Fonts/ now joins that: the app and the CLI set ProjectFonts.libraryFolders when they start, and every registration takes in what's new there, subfolders and a linked folder included. So a title in a shared font draws in the app, tandem serve and a CLI export alike, and a preset font Mike keeps in the library isn't downloaded into the project again. assets use of a shared font says it stays in the library until the project is archived.

title: Safer segments and shared conversions, from a review of the shared library
paragraphs: A segment named ". .." came out as "..", which is the library itself, and replacing it would have sent the whole Tandem Library to the Trash. Folder names now lose leading dots and spaces until none are left, and a segment is only ever saved directly inside Segments.

Replacing a segment kept nothing of the old one, but projects it went into play its files from the library. The new folder now keeps every file only the old version had (clones, so the old folder is untouched until the end); the old one is moved aside, the new one in, and what's left of the old one goes to the Trash, or back in place if the move fails. A save cut short is tidied by the next save of that name. Moving a segment to the Trash in the app asks first and says what it does to those projects.

A changed WebM or Lottie sticker was converted over the copy projects play, so a conversion that failed (a broken file, a full disk) left them a missing file. The new copy is now made beside the old one and swapped in only when it's whole. Every rescan converts changed files a project uses, not only the app's watcher, so a change noticed at launch or by a CLI search isn't missed.

A segment's media items kept their source IDs, which for library assets are the same everywhere, so using that asset later placed the segment's copy instead. They're blank now, and inserting gives them fresh IDs. Loading a segment prefers its folder's name and refuses a name two segments share. Relink's automatic pass over the shared library only takes a file whose content matches.

title: Titles draw in their fonts wherever they render, and say so when they can't
paragraphs: The caption preset asks for Tilt Warp, which macOS doesn't have, so the workbench short's captions rendered in SF Pro and nothing said so. `tandem assets use fontsource:tilt-warp` with the app open registered the font for the CLI's own process only, and the app registered fonts at launch and when it opened a project, so its renders stayed in SF Pro until a restart. And a CLI render of a project the app didn't have open (frame, clip, export) never registered the project's assets/font/ at all, so the workbench's own Tilt Warp copy was ignored there too.

Every composition build now registers the files in the project's assets/font/ this process hasn't seen first (ProjectFonts), in the app, `tandem serve` and CLI commands alike, and drops cached title drawings when a font arrives. The app's viewer builds again when any font is registered in its process, and the app looks for new ones when its window comes to the front and on a media refresh. `tandem status` and `validate` register them before they check, and `assets use` of a font asks the app for its status, so the app has the font straight away and the output says so.

A title in a font this process can't draw is a warning with the fix in the render's warnings (the viewer's status bar, frame, clip, export) and in captions, status and validate: "Tilt Warp, the caption preset's font, isn't installed, so 101 text clips are drawn in SF Pro instead. Install it with: tandem assets use fontsource:tilt-warp". A fontsource ID now works in `assets use` without a search first, so that command runs as given.

The caption preset names its font's asset. The first time a project needs a preset font it doesn't have (captions applied, a frame, clip or export of a title using it, the app showing one), PresetFonts installs it from the asset library's Fontsource provider into assets/font/, one download at a time and not again for two minutes after one fails.

A headless `tandem frame` of a clone of the Workbench Short drew its Tilt Warp titles and captions in SF Pro before and in Tilt Warp now. With the clone's assets/font/ hidden its 7 frames are byte for byte the same as before and each warns that TiltWarp-Regular isn't installed, and the 10 decision-models v14 frames are unchanged.

title: A title's own style wins over its preset, even when it's the default
paragraphs: On the workbench short a label with "style": {"uppercase": false} still rendered GITHUB.COM/MIKECANN/WORKBENCH, and a callout with strokeWidth 0 and shadow false kept both, because ResolvedText only used a clip's value when it differed from the TextStyle() default. Every text clip also wrote a full style, so a caption's JSON read SF Pro Display, 64, 800 though its preset decided.

TextStyle's fields are optional now. A field a clip sets wins over its preset, whatever the value; one it doesn't set comes from the preset, then TextStyle.defaults (TitlePresets.style(for:)). Only set fields are written and an empty style not at all, so a caption is its preset, its words and --y. animationDuration works the same way, "none" switches a preset's animation off (splitting a preset title used to bring its fades back at the cut; now there's none), and a see-through backgroundColor switches a preset's box off.

The project schema goes to 2. Schema 1 read a stored default as "not set", so loading a schema 1 file drops style values equal to the old defaults (and a 0.4 s animation length) and every title looks as it did; only values set from now on win. Journal entries and headless undo snapshots an older build wrote are read the same way, and an older build refuses a schema 2 file rather than dropping what it can't read.

The Filmora importer sets what Filmora says, captions, templates and library drops set nothing, `tandem timeline` lists the fields a title sets itself (style uppercase=false shadow=false), and the schema says how it works. The Text inspector shows the values a title is drawn with, puts the clip's own in amber with a button back to the preset's, and gains Outline and Capitals rows; None on a callout's background now switches its box off.

Frames from clones of the Workbench Short (7 times) and decision-models v14 (4 times, and 6 more with its Text track moved on top so its callout and version titles show, mid-animation too) are byte for byte the same as before. Setting uppercase false on the workbench's label now renders it in lower case.

title: The Text tab's four sub-tabs fit a narrow library panel
paragraphs: With Segments beside Titles, Templates and Fonts the row no longer fit the narrowest library panel (240 pt) and Segments came out cut short. The row now steps down, closer together and without the count, then in a point smaller type, whichever fits. The MCP server's instructions point agents at segments_list and segments_insert, and the Stickers README says a WebM or Lottie sticker is converted when Tandem first shows it.

title: Transcript words sit on the voice, and a word a cut runs through shows once
paragraphs: SpeechAnalyzer times its words end to end, so every pause hides inside a word: on the workbench short's phone take "of" ran from 28.14 to 29.22 s over a silence from 28.26 to 29.05. `tandem pauses --min 0.45` found 4 of the take's pauses, and after 24 cuts made in pauses the captions said 18 words twice, because a word a cut ran through showed on both sides of it.

Transcripts are now aligned to the file's cached waveform when they're read (TranscriptAlignment). A threshold 10 dB over the take's noise floor finds the silences (the waveform finds the same 45 that silencedetect does at -32 dB, to 10 ms, so it needed no new envelope), and each word goes to the voiced run its own range overlaps most, leaning past the pause after a sentence ends. Because it runs at read time, transcripts already in a cache get it without being transcribed again. The job now stores the engine's own times and rawTranscript(for:) returns them. Asking for a transcript asks for the waveform too.

Everything that puts words on the timeline places them by one rule, Transcript.placements(on:): among one track's clips of the file, a word shows once, on the clip that plays most of it (measured in media time, so speed doesn't change it), and not at all when less than half of it is left. Captions, pauses, tighten, search, transcript, timeline --words, the app's transcript lane and its Tighten pauses popover all use it; the popover now finds pauses the way `tandem pauses` does, across cuts too.

On a copy of the workbench project the uncut take has 21 pauses of 0.45 s or more (was 4), holding all 16 that silencedetect finds between words, and `captions` plans exactly the 257 words the session corrected its captions to by hand (was 275).

title: A phone video of someone talking is the camera take, and a Live Photo is one media item
paragraphs: `tandem new` on the workbench short's folder added source/IMG_0151.MOV, an iPhone selfie of Mike talking, as `other`, so it had no transcript until its role was set by hand. And photos exported from Photos doubled the media list: every Live Photo arrived as a HEIC plus a 1 to 3 second .mov, and each .mov was added as a video of its own.

A new video that nothing names now becomes the camera take when it's a recording with a voice and a face (CameraTakes). Its metadata has to name the camera that shot it, or it has to be in source/; Apple's sound classifier has to hear speech in a quarter of six sampled stretches; and Vision has to find a face a tenth of the frame high in two of six frames. Renders of an edit have a voice and a face too but no camera make or model, so the renders, drafts and previews in Mike's Filmora-era folders stay `other`, and a phone clip of the build guide talked over has no face and stays `other` as well. `tandem new` prints each camera take with its reason and the updateMedia that changes it, or, with none, the command to make the longest video with sound the camera.

A Live Photo's still is now the media item, with the movie's path in the new optional MediaItem.livePhotoVideo, and the movie isn't added. A pair is a HEIC or JPEG and a .mov with one name in one folder, confirmed by Apple's content identifier when both carry one, otherwise by the movie being 5 s or less with no alpha. Folder scans (tandem new, tandem media --refresh, the app's watcher) and files dropped on the app pair them; a drop puts the movie beside its still. A movie a project already has as media is left alone, and `tandem media` shows each still's motion clip.

On clones of the workbench short's source/ and photos/, `tandem new --portrait` adds 16 items where it added 29: 13 stills with their motion clips, two phone videos and IMG_0151.MOV as the camera take, "an Apple iPhone XS Max video with speech and a face in it".

title: Exports stay under -1 dBTP after AAC encoding
paragraphs: The limiter held the mix at -1.1 dBTP, but AAC overshoots a limited peak, so finished files measured over the ceiling with ffmpeg: the workbench short's draft came out at -1.01 dBTP. On synthetic hits that keep the limiter busy, the file measured 0.1 to 0.4 dB over the mix at 320 kbps and up to 1.1 dB at 256.

The limiter now aims 0.5 dB under the preset's ceiling, on top of its own 0.1 dB, in the loudness passes and the encode alike, so the gain search still lands on the target. A copy of the workbench short measures -14.0 LUFS and -1.5 dBTP with ffmpeg's ebur128 (-1.51 with loudnorm). The export reports the mix before AAC, which now reads -1.6 dBTP.

title: Export presets set the quality, and the project sets the shape
paragraphs: A 1080x1920 project (tandem new --portrait) couldn't be exported as a short. --preset short asked for a "portrait" format that only landscape projects get, the default export rendered it at the 4K preset's 80 Mbps (752 MB for 76 s), and --preset youtube1080 laid it out again as 1920x1080 without a word.

A preset now gives a codec, a bitrate and a resolution class (the frame's short side), and the frame keeps the canvas's shape. ExportPreset.plan(for:) works out the frame (the canvas or an alternate format), the size and the bitrate, and the CLI, the API, the exporter and the app's Export dialog all go through it:

- On a 1080x1920 canvas youtube1080 is 1080x1920 and youtube4k is 2160x3840, with a warning that it's upscaled. 4K landscape projects export as before. A 1920x1080 project now defaults to youtube1080, and youtube4k upscales it.
- --preset short renders the portrait format, or the canvas when that's 9:16, and otherwise fails with an error that names tandem short --apply. tandem short refuses a canvas that's already 9:16, since it's the short already.
- With no preset the canvas decides: youtube1080 for a canvas 1080 or less on its short side, youtube4k for anything bigger.
- Bitrates are for a 16:9 frame at up to 30 fps. A square gets 56% of the bits, and 48 to 60 fps gets half as much again, as in YouTube's table. The rates stay: H.264 1080p at 20 Mbps and HEVC 4K at 80 are about 2.5 times YouTube's recommendations, which is headroom for a speed-priority hardware encoder, and what Mike's Filmora presets used. Audio goes from 256 to 320 kbps, the most Apple's AAC encoder takes (YouTube asks for 384).
- Every export prints the preset, size, codec and bitrate it used.
- The Export dialog shows each preset's size for the open project, opens on the one that fits and explains a short it can't make.

tandem help export says which preset suits which project, and AGENTS.md's short recipe covers a project made portrait as well as a short cut from a landscape one. On a copy of the workbench short, the default, short and youtube1080 exports each came out 1080x1920 H.264 at 20 Mbps, 192 MB and -14.0 LUFS.

title: A segment's library assets stay in the credits of every video it goes into
paragraphs: A segment copies its files, so a Noto sticker or a licensed sound in an intro would have dropped out of the description credits of the videos the intro went into. When a segment is saved, each clip whose file or look came from the asset library (the catalogue's record of what the project used) now carries that asset's ID as an asset:<id> tag, and the credits count every asset a clip on the timeline names that way. The tags travel with the clips through inserting, archiving and copying, and go when the clip does.

title: Segments keep the transitions between their clips
paragraphs: A Template can now carry transitions, naming its clips by their place in clips: between two of them on one track, or at one clip's head or tail. insertTemplate adds them once the clips are in, through addTransition, so the usual handle checks hold, and refuses one that joins clips on two tracks or a clip the template hasn't. A saved segment keeps every transition whose clips are all in it (an intro card fading up from black, a dissolve into the next card) and notes the ones to a clip it left out.
Also: inserting a segment in the app leaves a warning the edit had on screen, and the save sheet's copy runs with the store as a constant.

title: The shared library in Settings and the tabs, and Save selection as segment
paragraphs: The app makes ~/Movies/Tandem Library the first time it opens after installing (never from the tests), registers the fonts in its Fonts folder, watches it and rescans it at launch. A file dropped in shows up in its tab with a "Shared library" chip, and its thumbnail is made as its tile comes into view; a changed file a project uses is converted again. Tandem > Settings shows where the library is and moves it (the choice goes in the asset library's settings, so the CLI follows it).

Timeline > Save selection as segment, and the same item on a clip's menu, open a sheet that names the selection after its first title, lets Mike mark titles whose words change each time, and saves it with copies of its files into Segments. Segments show in the Text tab beside the templates, since they are templates: a group of clips that go in together, linked, with words that can change, next to the built-in Like and Subscribe and Comment Below they generalise. The Graphics tab places single files. Each tile sketches the segment's tracks; double-clicking puts it at the playhead and dragging drops it through the template path, which now finds segments too, so the timeline's drop code is unchanged.

A project that opens with media missing looks in this Mac's shared library after its own folder, so one from another Mac finds its stickers and sounds. The CLI and MCP look at the shared library again before they search, so a file dropped in is found with the app closed.
ASSETS.md has the shared library and the reference and copy rules, ARCHITECTURE.md where shared files go when a project is archived, and AGENTS.md the segments commands and a recipe.

title: Video and Audio sliders reset on a double-click and explain themselves
paragraphs: The Colour tab's sliders already did. Scale and opacity go back to 100%, crop, fades and voice isolation to 0, the cutout edge to 2 px, a transition to its type's usual length and the speech level to -20 LUFS. Every row's tooltip says what it does and how to reset it, and the number's says it can be dragged or typed.

title: The copy grade line reads right when every file matches
paragraphs: It said "Every other camera files has this grade" in the menu's own larger type. When the other files already match it's now a quiet line ("The other 2 camera files have this grade too."), and otherwise an amber "Copy grade to…" menu like the Effects tab's "+ Add".

title: URL commands can name the project they're for
paragraphs: With two projects open and Tandem in the background, the "front" window is whichever was last main, so a check meant for one project landed on the other. `project=` takes a window title, file name or path, and a name that isn't open does nothing rather than falling back to the front window.

title: A shared library folder, used where it is, archived with the project
paragraphs: Mike wanted one place on this Mac for the stickers, graphics, sounds, music, looks, fonts and reusable bits of timeline every video uses, and for archiving to make a project standalone again before it goes to Bruce. SharedLibrary is that folder, ~/Movies/Tandem Library unless the settings move it (and inside the asset library's own folder for tests and $TANDEM_ASSETS_ROOT, so they never touch the real one). It makes itself with Stickers, Graphics, Sound effects, Music, Looks, Fonts and Segments and a README in each, and never writes over a README Mike edited.

Its files join the asset library as the "shared" source, through the import folder indexing, which now lets a provider say how its files are found: a file's folder says what it is (a short sound in Music is still music), Segments and the READMEs are left out, the nearest tandem-licence.json above a file covers it, and IDs are the path inside the library, so they survive the folder moving. A row whose file is somewhere else now (the library moved) is described again.

Using a shared asset refers to the file where it is instead of copying it into assets/, so improving a sticker there improves every project that uses it. Files a project can't play as they are (WebM, Lottie, SVG, animated GIF) play from the library's converted copy, which is made again when the file changes and a project uses it. Audio is measured but never copied to a 48 kHz WAV. Downloaded and import folder assets are still copied, as before.

Archiving copies every shared file a project uses into it: media into media/Tandem Library/<where it was in the library>, a converted copy named after its sticker, LUTs into assets/lut and fonts from Fonts/ into assets/font (the CLI looks there too, since only the app registers them). Links are followed both ways: a library that is itself a link, a link in the project folder into the library, and a library file that links elsewhere all count as outside and are copied as real files. Relink looks in the shared library after the folders it's given.

Segments: SegmentMaker turns clips into a Template with optional fields and copies every file they play, and their LUTs, beside segment.json in Segments/<name>/, whole or not at all. A template clip can now carry the media item it needs, so inserting a segment is one insertTemplate that adds the library files the project lacks and reuses the ones it has. tandem segments list/save/insert and the segments_* MCP tools do this for agents; transitions between the clips aren't kept yet, and saving says so.

title: Copy a take's grade to the other camera files
paragraphs: The Colour tab's whole-take view gets a "Copy grade to…" menu: every other file like this one (camera files for a camera take, never a screen recording) or one at a time, with the ones that already match ticked. Each copy gets its own effect IDs and the whole copy is one undo.

title: Keyframed colour wheel hues blend the short way round
paragraphs: A hue keyframed from 350 to 10 swept through green and blue on its way to red. Wheel hues are angles, so their keyframes now take the shorter arc and land in 0 to 360. Other numbers, rotation included, still move in a straight line, since a rotation from 350 to 10 is a real spin.

title: Files dropped from Finder above or below the tracks get a new track
paragraphs: Library media already did this. Files that fit the new track (picture on a video track, sound on an audio track) go on it one after another, and the rest are placed as usual. The track's ID is made once per drop so a retried commit doesn't add a second track.

title: Transcript phrases end in an ellipsis at the edge, and each project keeps its own window frame
paragraphs: Since the lanes draw in tiles, a transcript phrase running past the right edge was cut off mid-word; tiles draw phrases whole and don't know where the edge is. A small overlay at the end of the transcript lane now fades the phrase into an ellipsis whenever one runs past, as before.

With two projects open (Decision Models and the workbench short), both windows shared one saved frame, so they came back stacked. Frames are now kept per project file, falling back to the last window's frame for a project that hasn't got one yet.

title: The Colour tab's whole take previews while it's dragged
paragraphs: The viewer's live drag overrides stood in only for a clip's own properties, so dragging a slider or a wheel on the whole take (the file's look, where Mike grades a camera take) showed nothing until it was let go. LiveVideoOverrides now carries looks by media ID as well. The compositor uses one in place of the file's look for every clip of that file, and set([:]) ends it with the rest, once the composition with the committed look is on screen. The Colour tab hands over the dragged look together with the clip's own properties, unchanged, and those are what have the viewer redraw.

The colour tests now let their editor models and offscreen windows finish with the main thread before the next test starts. After them the frame pacer's timing test failed about one run in four; now it doesn't.

title: Proxies of big overlays keep their alpha, so the viewer shows the track below
paragraphs: ProxyJob read every video as 4:2:0 and wrote plain HEVC, so with Proxy on the viewer played a black box behind an HEVC-with-alpha overlay bigger than 1080p, or the colour straight alpha hides under the clear parts for ProRes 4444 and converted QuickTime Animation stickers. Paused frames and exports, read from the originals, were right.

Video with alpha is now read as BGRA and proxied as HEVC with alpha. The encoder takes straight or premultiplied from the frames' tag, so the proxy blends like the original. Only those proxies change: their cache key gains "alpha":"1", retiring any opaque one, and the proxy version stays 3, so camera and screen proxies keep their files.
A 10 s 4K ProRes 4444 overlay proxies in 1.4 s to 15.5 MB and decodes at 1,135 fps against the original's 393.

title: A simulated hover can hold a key, to check the zoom cursor
WebM stickers keep their colours in the asset library
paragraphs: VP8 and VP9 WebMs went to ProRes with no colour tags, and the HEVC export guessed: SMPTE-C for a small picture (red came out 245, 33, 0), BT.709 for a big one (a Filmora sticker's greens 25 levels high). The ProRes frames are now tagged with the WebM's own tags where AVFoundation reads them, otherwise BT.709 primaries and transfer with the BT.601 matrix ffmpeg and browsers use for untagged RGB. VP9's BT.601 flag (bt470bg) is tagged smpte170m, the code AVFoundation reads, and full range is scaled to limited.

title: The debug dump gives each view's rectangle in simulate's coordinates
The Colour tab redraws only what an edit changes
paragraphs: Every edit rebuilt all thirty-odd controls in the tab. Each one held closures over a copy of the project, which SwiftUI can't compare, so it couldn't skip any. Sections and controls now take plain values and a small editor handle that reads the clip and the look at the moment a change is made. SwiftUI skips whatever an edit didn't touch, and a control that wasn't redrawn can't write back an older grade.

On a 300-clip project in a release build, an edit plus the tab's update and layout takes 5.0 ms with every section open (was 6.9) and 0.8 ms with them all collapsed (was 1.8). The mixer's share halved. For comparison, the old tab took 0.5 to 0.8 ms with its effect rows closed and 5.3 to 7.5 ms with them open. What's left is SwiftUI's layout pass. ColourInspectorTiming measures it (TANDEM_COLOUR_TIMING=1).
Dragging a slider, a wheel or a number on "This clip" now sets model.videoPreview, which the viewer's live drag overrides draw from. A drag that ends where it started shows the clip as it was.

Double-clicking a slider's label resets it too. Values at "no change" are drawn faint so the changed ones stand out, and a wheel's puck moves at half the pointer's speed so a subtle grade is easy to hit. Sliders add tooltips only when they're given one, so a .help set around a SliderRow (as the Audio tab's level rows do) still shows.

title: Cursors that say what a press does
paragraphs:
- Viewer: the selection box's corner handles show their diagonal resize arrows, the selected layer shows a hand (closed while moving it), and holding Z shows the zoom cursor.
- Timeline: the cursor comes from the drag a press would start, so clip edges show a trim arrow, the roll tool shows a column arrow on a cut between two clips, slip and slide show a hand, the blade tool has a scissors cursor, keyframes a pointing hand, and a locked track only the arrow. Drags keep their cursor, and changing the tool updates it.
- Ruler markers show a hand, lane edges the row resize cursor.
- One tested place picks them all (CursorKind), and tandem://debug reports the current cursor so simulated hovers can be checked.

title: Menus with icons and keys, drops where they're let go, and a click takes the playhead to the clip
paragraphs: The right-click menus on clips, tracks, keyframes, transitions and the viewer get icons, and show a key where the item does exactly what the key does (Delete, Ripple delete, Link, the layouts, Mark clip, Safe margins). Cut here cuts at the pointer and the key at the playhead, so it gets an icon only.

A title dropped on the timeline went to the Text track wherever it was let go. It now goes on the video track under the pointer (the Text track if that's a sound track). Dropping above the top video track makes a new video track on top for it, and dropping media below the last track makes a new audio track at the bottom for its sound, as Filmora does (DropTarget, placeMediaOnNewTrack). The preview shows the new track, and the label says so.
A plain click on a clip moves the playhead to its start, so the viewer shows what was picked, unless the playhead is on the clip already.

The render tests' movie writer drew into the asset writer's pixel buffer pool, which a writer failing under load tears down while the writer block may still be using it: an occasional crash in CVPixelBufferPoolCreatePixelBuffer, seen once in LevelRenderTests with the machine loaded. It draws into its own buffers now, so a failing writer shows up as its error instead.

title: Timeline thumbnails ready for the screen
paragraphs: Profiling a zoom with the whole edit in view, most of each frame went on Core Animation converting every thumbnail from sRGB to the monitor's colour profile and resampling it to the size drawn, and the main thread waited for that before it could show the frame. Thumbnails are now redrawn once, off the main thread, at the pixels they cover and in the window's colour space, so drawing one is a copy. They look the same (3 levels at most).

Zooming with the whole edit in view, medians of two runs: 1.03 s of main-thread time -> 0.59 s, the slowest frame 67 ms -> 21 ms and the 95th percentile 29 ms -> 10 ms. Zooming at 20 points a second: 0.65 s -> 0.56 s.
Transcripts are read from the analysis cache once too: a drag's preview decoded them from disk on every frame.

title: The timeline lanes paint in tiles that move when scrolling
paragraphs: The lanes paint into tiles 512 points of time wide. Scrolling moves them, so only what scrolls into view paints, plus a strip along the left edge where the labels of clips that start off screen stay in view (as wide as what's pinned there, about 240 points on the demo). Zooming, or dragging a track's height, paints one full-size canvas instead of every tile, and the tiles come back when it rests: six layers a step cost a third more than one. Painting works in content coordinates (LanesPainter) on whole points, so tiles, strip and canvas give the same pixels, and clip edges on exact frame times no longer move a point with rounding.

An edit, and each move of a drag or drop's preview, repaints only the clips it changed (TimelineDamage.previewRects), and the snap line and drag label are layers of their own. Dragging a title in from the Text library worked out the drop and rebuilt the snap targets on every mouse move, found the previewed clips by searching every track for every clip, and repainted all the lanes. It now works out a drop once per frame, track and clip under the pointer, and repaints what changed.
Updates are paced to the screen's frame rate (FramePacer): a 125 Hz mouse drew twice per frame, and each frame waited for the screen to let go of the one before.

Main-thread time on the demo project in a 2560 wide window, medians of two runs, before the last commit, after it, and now:
- a pan with the whole edit in view: 2.62 s, 1.99 s -> 0.42 s, the slowest frame 125 ms, 49 ms -> 13 ms
- a 125 Hz middle-button pan: 0.61 s, 0.68 s -> 0.40 s
- a 60 Hz trackpad scroll: 0.80 s, 0.68 s -> 0.55 s
- zooming: about the same (0.64 s -> 0.65 s) A clip drag's preview repaints under a tenth of the lanes per move (TimelineRedrawTests), and zooming paints the canvas then the tiles.
tandem://simulate takes dragover (stay=1 leaves the preview up) for timing drags from the libraries.

Screenshots of fifteen states (scrolls, zooms, a drop's preview, a drag and drop, undo, clicks) match the old drawing pixel for pixel, except that a fractional scroll lands on the nearest whole point and a transcript phrase running off the right edge is cut by it instead of ending in an ellipsis.

title: The timeline redraws only what changed
paragraphs: On macOS 26 AppKit watches the @Observable values a view's draw(_:) reads and redraws the whole view when any of them changes. The lanes read the playhead to highlight the transcript, so while playing all 2448 by 749 points of them redrew 60 times a second. The ruler, headers and lanes also redrew in full on every scroll, zoom and click. They now draw from a copy of the model's state made when it changes (TimelineDrawState), and TimelineDamage works out what each change touches: a sideways scroll redraws the ruler and lanes but not the headers, a selection change only the clips whose selected or linked state changed, and the transcript only when the highlighted phrase changes. Mouse ups, clicks that don't move and the end of a drop no longer redraw everything.

The inspector and viewer read the timeline's scale just to name a clip, so every scroll and zoom step re-rendered both in SwiftUI, and the zoom slider re-rendered on every scroll. Names come from ClipRenderer.name(of:in:) now, and zoom and scroll are stored apart.

Labels pin to the lanes' left edge whatever part is being drawn (they pinned to the edge of the dirty rect, which partial redraws would have shown), and waveforms and volume lines sample on a grid from the clip's start, so a partial redraw lines up with what's around it.

Main-thread time on the demo project in a 2560 wide window, medians of two runs: 3.5 s of playback 1.86 s -> 0.68 s (the lanes redrew 346 times, now none), ten clicks on clips 0.48 s -> 0.23 s, a 60 Hz trackpad scroll 0.82 s -> 0.69 s. TimelineRedrawTests pins it: moving the playhead redraws nothing, a click redraws its clips, a scroll leaves the headers alone.

title: Archives keep the converted copies of stickers macOS can't decode
paragraphs: They're small, and making them again needs ffmpeg, which the Mac opening the archive may not have.

title: QuickTime Animation and PNG stickers play from an HEVC copy instead of failing renders
paragraphs: Stock alpha stickers (Storyblocks, Motion Array, older VideoHive) ship as QuickTime Animation or PNG in a MOV. macOS 26 has no decoder for either, so one such clip failed every frame grab and export with "Cannot Decode".

- The media probe asks AVFoundation whether the video decodes (isDecodable) and records the codec in MediaItem.undecodableCodec.
- A new `converted` analysis makes an HEVC copy with the alpha kept: ffmpeg to ProRes 4444, then the HEVC-with-alpha export preset (HEVCTranscoder, now shared with the asset library's WebM path). RGB frames are converted with BT.709 and tagged; untagged, the export guessed SMPTE-C and turned red orange.
- Thumbnails, proxies and mattes of such a file come from the copy.
- Frame grabs and exports convert what they need before building; the viewer leaves the clip out with a warning until the copy lands. A source that still can't be decoded is loaded without its video instead of failing the whole composition.
- The asset library converts these MOVs on import, like WebM.
- tandem media shows the codec and the conversion state, with the reason when an analysis fails. FFmpeg moved into TandemMedia.

title: File > Archive project…, and a relink prompt when media is missing
paragraphs: Archive project… opens a sheet on the project window with a dry run of the choice: what comes in from outside the folder and its size, anything missing, fonts copied, and for a copy the project folder's size and what's left out. It copies the project to another folder (Bruce's archive share, remembered for next time) or makes this folder standalone, shows a progress bar with Stop while it copies, and says where the archive went when it's done, with Show in Finder. It runs ProjectArchiver on the window's own session, the same work as `tandem archive`. The menu item goes down the responder chain like Show project in Finder, with its icon from Icons.menuImage.

When a project opens with media missing, files moved within its folder are relinked straight away, and a sheet lists the rest with Search a folder…, which relinks what it finds there and asks again if some are still missing. It waits until the window is in front, so a project opened in the background by a script isn't held up by it.

title: The picture follows a viewer drag live, and the viewer zooms out and about the pointer
paragraphs: Dragging a picture in picture in the viewer moved only its outline: the player kept drawing the committed composition until mouse up, and a composition takes 150 to 280 ms to rebuild, far too slow to redo per move. The render scene now carries LiveVideoOverrides, which the compositor reads for each layer on every frame. The viewer hands it the drag's properties (model.videoPreview, which the inspector's sliders set too), and a paused player draws its frame again, one at a time with only the latest waiting. The overrides stay until the composition with the committed edit is on screen, so the picture doesn't flick back.

The viewer zooms from a quarter of fit to eight times, about the pointer with a pinch or Command or Option and the wheel, and the wheel pans away from fit. The transport's zoom menu gains 25% and 50% and follows a pinch. The frame's edge is outlined, so what's in the video stays clear when zoomed out; double-click still fits.

title: Archive a project, standalone in its own folder or copied to the archive
paragraphs: A project could use files from outside its folder: an import's absolute paths, a sound from another video's folder, a LUT, a font only installed on this Mac, or a link in the folder to a file somewhere else. `tandem archive` (and the archive operation over HTTP and MCP) finds them in the project and in the other .tandem files beside it, copies them into media/<the folder they were in>/, assets/lut/ and assets/font/, and points the project at the copies as one undo step through the coordinator. With --to <folder> it writes a standalone copy of the whole folder there instead and leaves the original alone. The copy leaves out proxies, mattes, thumbnails and isolated voice (unless --with-cache) and node_modules; transcripts, waveforms and loudness always go, and their cache keys still match because copies keep their modification dates.

Copies are copyfile clones where they can be, otherwise full copies read back and checked by SHA-256. Each file is copied once, a different file with the same name is never replaced (the copy goes beside it as "name 2"), and copies wait under hidden names until they're checked, so a run stopped part way changes nothing in the project and the next one carries on from there. archive.json records each file's original location, size, date and checksum, and each run. Missing files are listed and left as they are. `tandem relink --search <folder>` finds missing media by name and content. A copy of the decision-models demo brings in its 19 outside files (2.9 GB) in about a second and a half on one volume, and the archived copy validates with every path relative.

title: The Audio tab shows how a clip is levelled, and sets the speech level
paragraphs: The Normalise switch levelled a clip to the master's -14 LUFS. It now uses the project's speech level and says which ("to −20 LUFS"). The Measured row shows what normalising adds ("−32.7 LUFS · +12.7 dB to −20"), a Plays at row the result with the clip gain on top ("about −18.0 LUFS" with +2 dB), and a line under them says how the two combine and that export brings the whole mix to −14 LUFS.

A Project speech level section sets the level for the whole project (clips normalised to the old level follow it), says how many speech clips have a gain or level of their own, and has Normalise speech clips, which sets them all to the level in one undo step. Every control on the tab has a tooltip, the new section's icon comes from Icons, and the level sections live in their own file so the inspector's other tabs stay untouched.

title: Filmora imports level speech like placing does, --keep-levels for Filmora's own
paragraphs: The Filmora import read LoudnessGain as a plain gain on the raw file, but Filmora adds it after its Auto Normalization, which levels a file to about -24 LUFS on Tandem's meter (Filmora says -23). Measured on v14's export against its sources, 62 voice clips from three takes played at -24.1 LUFS plus their LoudnessGain (spread 0.7 dB), while the music played at its plain VolumeGain. So every imported voice sat 8 dB lower against the music and sound effects than Filmora played it.

Imports now normalise speech (the camera's sound, the Voice tracks, the rendered intro) to the project's speech level with no gain, the way placing does, which is about where Filmora had it; music and sound effects keep their Filmora volume. The report says so, with the range of gains it replaced. `tandem import filmora --keep-levels` keeps Filmora's own levels instead: Auto Normalization becomes normalizeTo -24 with the clip's gain on top. On v14 that matches the voice, but not the intro, whose LoudnessGain level_voice.py added and Filmora didn't apply.

The decision-models recipe put the voice and intro at -28.74 LUFS, the target build_wfp.py gave LoudnessGain on the same misreading. It now leaves them at the speech level, where v14 played them (voice -20.4, intro -18.8).

title: A Colour tab like other editors', with colour wheels
paragraphs: Mike found the Colour tab hard to use: the HSL effect opened out as 24 identical sliders with their names cut short, nothing like the colour panels he knows from other editors.

The tab now starts with a switch between the whole take (the file's look, how Mike grades a camera take, and where camera clips open) and this clip. Below it are fixed sections in grading order, each with an icon, a reset, an on/off switch and a chevron: Light (exposure, contrast, highlights, shadows, black level), Colour (temperature on a blue to amber track, tint green to magenta, saturation and vibrance grey to colour), Colour wheels, a Lightroom-style colour mixer (eight swatches with a dot on the changed ones, and the hue, saturation and luminance of the one picked on tracks of its colour), Vignette, Sharpen and LUT. A section's effect is added by its first change, reset takes it away, and switching a section off turns its effect off. Light and Colour share one colorAdjust, as Filmora imports have them, until one is switched off while the other has values; then they split in two. Anything the sections can't show is listed after them as it is, so nothing in a grade is hidden.

Colour wheels are a new effect, colorWheels: shadows, midtones and highlights as lift, gamma and gain, each with a hue, an amount and a brightness. The wheels are laid out like a BT.709 vectorscope, and a hue pushes colours along the same line with no change in luma, so the puck points where the picture goes on a scope. The kernel works on the encoded values with BT.709 weights like the other colour effects, and clamps nothing, so values outside 0 to 1 stay finite and in order. A puck moves from where it is when dragged (Option for fine moves), and a double-click puts it back.

Sliders everywhere get gradient tracks, a double-click on the knob to reset, a value you can drag to scrub or click to type, units (EV, %, °), labels that are never cut short and tooltips that say what each control does. A knob moves from where it's grabbed instead of jumping under the pointer.

Keyframe diamonds stay on a clip's own colour values (one per wheel for its three), and a change to an animated value sets the keyframe at the playhead. Undo names read like "Contrast (whole take)" and "Turn off light".

Tests cover the wheels' geometry, the kernel on colour patches read back in float, the section-to-effect mapping and its edit commands, the controls driven with mouse events in an offscreen window, and the tab rendered in each state (TANDEM_COLOUR_UI_OUT writes PNGs). The effects catalogue, the edit schema and AGENTS.md list colorWheels.

title: Speech is normalised to the project's speech level, -20 LUFS
paragraphs: Mike noticed none of his clips had Normalise on: the demo came from a Filmora import, which copied each voice take's hand-set gain. A project now has one speech level, settings.speechLoudness (-20 LUFS), and export still masters the whole mix to -14 LUFS under -1 dBTP.

Placing camera or voice sound, or anything on a take track like Voice, normalises it to the speech level with no gain, so the app, the CLI, MCP and the HTTP API all do the same; it used to normalise speech to the master's -14. Music (-31 dB) and sound effects (-15 dB) keep their gains. normalizeSpeech sets every speech clip to the speech level and clears its gain in one undo step, leaving fades, voice isolation, gain keyframes and locked tracks alone. Changing speechLoudness moves the clips normalised to the old level with it.

The render, tandem loudness and the app share one sum in AudioLevels: the target minus the file's measured loudness, within 30 dB either way, then the clip gain. A silent file now gets nothing instead of a "not measured" warning, and tandem loudness clamps like the render and says how many speech clips aren't at the level. A test checks the viewer's mix against the export's.

Why -20: Filmora's Auto Normalization, on for the voice in all of Mike's Filmora projects, levels a file to about -24 LUFS before his +2 to +4 dB, so his voice played at about -20 (v14's export: voice -20.4, mix -20.1), and the music and SFX gains came from those projects. It's the quiet end of the -16 to -20 AES recommends for speech. And the viewer plays the mix before the master: at -20 the demo's voice stays under 0 dBFS but for 4 clips by up to 2 dB, where -16 clips 58 by up to 6 dB.

On a copy of the v14 demo normalizeSpeech moves 230 clips, the export still measures -14.0 LUFS and -1.1 dBTP, and the voice sits 23.7 dB over the music in pauses, against 25.9 in Filmora's own export and 18.0 with the copied gains. Older projects load with -20; there's no schema bump, since clips keep their own normalizeTo and an older build that drops the setting only resets the level for new clips.

title: The inspector's tab bar and project header span the panel again
paragraphs: The tab row sized to its tabs once it could switch to icons alone, so its divider stopped short; the project header's divider always had.

title: Tooltips that name the shortcut, and menus that show every key
paragraphs: Mike wants to learn the shortcuts by using the app: hovering a tool should say what it is and its key, and menus should show keys wherever there is one.

Tooltips now come up after half a second instead of the system's second and a half, which is why the existing ones went unnoticed. The tools say what they do and their key ("Blade tool (B): click a clip to cut it there"), and the toggles, transport, zoom, library tabs and Export do the same, reading the live keymap (Shortcuts.help) so a custom keymap shows its own keys.

The menu bar showed only Command shortcuts, because a plain B as a menu key equivalent would take the b from a text field. It now shows plain keys too: EditorMainMenu lets keys without Command pass on to the window, where the keyboard router already runs them. Menu items get icons, NSMenu.add takes an icon and a command (for the key), and the media and asset context menus get icons.

title: Icons on the inspector's tabs and sections, and clip tabs that say they need a clip
paragraphs: Mike asked for small icons to make the panels easier to scan. The inspector tabs get one each (and fall back to icons alone, with the chosen tab's title, when the inspector is narrow), every section title gets one, the effect rows show their effect's icon, and the layout picker shows little layout pictures over its names.

With nothing selected (or a transition), clicking Video, Colour, Audio or Info changed nothing, since the panel shows the project. Those tabs are now dimmed and don't switch, a hover says to select a clip, and the project view says the same in words.
Icons live in Support/Icons.swift so the same thing always gets the same symbol, and the effect menus show them too.

title: Timing for how long the main thread is blocked
paragraphs: The draw timings said how long each view's draw(_:) took, but not how long the main thread was busy, which is what makes the app feel stuck: Core Animation's commit can wait on the screen after drawing is done. Every time the run loop wakes, the app now records how long it stays busy ("main thread busy") and how much of that goes on run loop observers, where SwiftUI updates, layout, drawing and the commit happen ("display"). tandem://debug?reset=1 clears the timings after writing them, so one gesture can be timed on its own, and the summary gives totals.

tandem://simulate?scroll= takes steps and interval, so a trackpad swipe or an Option-scroll zoom can be replayed at a steady pace like a drag. tandem://window?order=front or back moves the window without activating the app. A copy of the app built under another bundle ID and URL scheme answers its own links, so it can be measured beside the installed one.

title: The media list stops asking the disk about transcripts on every redraw
paragraphs: Each take's "Transcribed" badge looked its transcript up in the analysis cache whenever the list redrew, which goes to the disk (the fingerprint and cache folder lookups): about 20 ms a click with four takes listed, found by the timeline performance session. The answer is now kept per take until the analysis results change (artworkRevision), which is also what redraws the badge when a transcript lands, and it asks isCached rather than decoding the transcript.

title: Dividers that are easy to grab, and side panels that resize
paragraphs: The one divider that dragged (between the workspace and the timeline) could be grabbed on 4 points and only changed the pointer over its 1 point line, so it was hard to find. The two between the side panels and the viewer didn't drag at all.

All three are now the same divider: a 1 point line with an 11 point grab band over the panels' edges, a resize pointer across the whole band, and an amber highlight while it's hovered or dragged. The media panel (240 to 560 points) and the inspector (300 to 600) resize, always leaving the viewer 420 points; a window too narrow for them takes the room back in proportion and gives it back when it widens. A double-click puts a panel back to its standard size, or the timeline split back to fitting every track. The sizes are kept in the app's preferences, so a restart keeps the layout.

The effects, titles and asset grids fit as many tiles as the panel has room for instead of a fixed three (or two) columns, and the line between two track headers grabs 5 points either side instead of 3.

title: Proxies with a keyframe every 15 frames, so still areas stop crawling
paragraphs: All-intra proxies made their compression noise anew every frame, and it crawled over still walls and screen text while playing: 8x8 blocks of the camera's wall changed 0.45 levels a frame at quality 0.6, against 0.13 in the original. Proxies now have P-frames with a keyframe every 15 frames (no reordering) at quality 0.78. The wall changes 0.067 a frame, with a tick of 0.31 at each keyframe, about the size of the camera's own keyframe tick (0.26; over 32x32 blocks 0.12 against its 0.14). Still screen text changes less than in the recording. Camera proxies are 97 MB a minute (were 105), screen recordings 11 (were 57), and they build as fast.

Exact seeks decode from the keyframe before: across the v14 edit the frame shows in 11.5 ms at p50 and 15.8 at p95, against 7.1 and 9.2 all-intra. A frame back is 14 ms at p95; a frame forward, drags and playing at any speed either way are unchanged. A keyframe every 30 frames saved little and dropped a quarter of the frames dragging backwards.

The keyframe interval is a proxy setting and part of the cache key with the quality, and the proxy version goes to 3 so all-intra proxies rebuild. ProxyExactFrameTests checks that seeks, arrow-key steps across keyframes and playback land on the exact frame; ProxyRealMediaTests pins the flicker, size and seek numbers on the demo footage. docs/RENDER.md has the tables.

title: Selection box outlines the right way up, link groups found once
paragraphs: The outline layer's path was flipped for a layer that was already flipped by a parent, so the outlines showed mirrored at the bottom of the lanes. It now asks the layer whether its contents are flipped.

What was left of a box drag's time went on finding link groups: one pass over every clip per boxed clip, copying each clip on the way. The box now finds them in two passes over the timeline, and linkedClipIDs(of:) no longer copies every clip to find a few.

title: The selection box outlines clips on a layer instead of redrawing
paragraphs: The box still redrew the lanes whenever it picked up or dropped a clip, which on a dense timeline is most mouse moves.
